AI-Simulated Expert Panels for
Socio-Technical Scenarios and Decision
Guidance
Socio-technical scenarios for net-zero and other transformation pathways
combine qualitative storylines with quantitative models, embedding them
in plausible societal contexts for model assessment. Conventional scenario
generation is resource-intensive, can be limited in internal consistency and
diversity of expert and stakeholder perspectives, and is rarely stress-tested.
This paper introduces a synthetic, AI-based expert panel to address these
bottlenecks. An AI model first simulates domain experts who agree on de-
scriptors, states, and their interactions. A probabilistic Cross-Impact Bal-
ance analysis then generates internally consistent pathways, using stochastic
shocks to assess robustness and pathway diversity. An AI stakeholder panel
uses multi-criteria decision analysis to select a preferred pathway; an AI
expert panel translates it into model-ready quantitative inputs. Although
scalable and applicable to any other country or region, the framework is
applied to Germany’s energy transition as a proof of concept, and offers
an alternative and/or supplement to scenario generation. Furthermore, it
enables Virtual AI-Led Decision Laboratories for exploratory policy stress-
testing and provides an approach for rapid, structured expert elicitation and
decision support in other domains.
Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Energy transition; Large language model;
Uncertainty quantification; Multi-agent systems
JEL Classification: Q40, C63, D81, O33

1. Introduction
Socio-technicalscenariosforenergy,climate,andrelatedtransformationanal-
ysis combine qualitative storylines about possible societal and policy futures
with quantitative modelling [1, 2]. This combination embeds future path-
ways within plausible societal contexts [3], giving quantitative analysis its
contextual meaning and policy relevance and making the assumptions be-
hind model results explicit for decision-makers [4]. The Cross-Impact Bal-
ance (CIB) method offers a formal framework for building these foresight
storylines [1]. Experts define descriptors and their alternative future states,
elicit cross-impacts in a cross-impact matrix (CIM), run the CIB consistency
analysis, select or prioritise scenarios (e.g. via multi-criteria decision analysis
(MCDA)), and convert the chosen storylines into quantitative assumptions
for sectoral models [1, 4, 5, 2, 6, 3]. The process is time- and resource-
intensive and constrains the number of descriptors and states that smaller
projects can afford [6].
Current limitations in expert-elicitation approaches that inform CIB [1],
MCDA, and the expert quantification of scenarios compound these con-
straints. These limitations fall into three areas: who participates, how de-
cisions are made, and how storylines are translated into numbers. Scenario
construction relies on small, purposively selected expert groups rather than
representative samples, so consensus ratings can reflect majority views or
group dynamics rather than the full range of expert or societal perspectives
[3, 7, 8]. The same applies to expert-led quantification and MCDA-based
selection [9, 10, 11]. The time and resources required can limit what infor-
mation is gathered and how much it can be refined [12]. It is often difficult
to trace how input decisions were reached [13].
In addition, subjectivity in assessments and group dynamics can significantly
influence outcomes, for example when consensus is determined by majority
opinion or by the influence of dominant individuals, whilst dissenting views
are rarely documented [14, 15, 16]. The conversion from qualitative story-
lines to model parameters still relies heavily on modeller interpretation and
can leave parameters only loosely tied to the narrative [7, 17]. Moreover,
ensuring internal consistency across complex systems is cognitively demand-
ing, whilst conventional panels often struggle to represent the full diversity of
stakeholder views (e.g. consumer, industry, environmental) owing to logisti-
1

cal constraints, potentially leading to narrow or technocratic selection biases
[3]. Despite these limitations, expert elicitation remains essential for consis-
tency, traceability, and making scenario logic explicit to decision-makers.
This paper presents a novel application of artificial intelligence (AI) to struc-
tured expert elicitation and decision-making to address and mitigate these
challenges. In this proposed framework, a single large language model (LLM)
simulates a multi-expert panel whenever expert consultation is required. It
generates the required inputs for CIB (descriptors, states, and the cross-
impact matrix), conducts a workshop that informs MCDA (e.g. criteria and
weightsforscenarioselection), andquantifiesthechosenscenarios(e.g.trans-
lating storylines into model parameters such as demand trajectories or car-
bon prices). Critically, the approach extends beyond scenario generation
to decision support. The AI-simulated stakeholder panel performs MCDA,
explicitly negotiating conflicting criteria (e.g. public acceptance versus in-
frastructure speed) to select pathways, thereby providing a transparent au-
dit trail of the value judgements underpinning scenario selection. The CIB
analysis implemented in this framework extends the prevailing workflow by
incorporating confidence-coded judgement uncertainty and structural and
dynamic shocks within a dynamic multi-period pathway framework, so that
both robustness and shock-induced state switching are explored alongside
the central workshop storyline (such aspects are often neglected in current
scenario practice [18, 19]).
Theapproachdelegatesthesekeyexpert-elicitationanddecision-makingsteps
to AI-simulated panels, and offers documented reasoning at each step, a re-
runnable protocol for iteration and sensitivity analysis, and lower time and
resource intensity than convening conventional workshops. The design allows
for facilitator or expert intervention at any stage, so that a hybrid work-
flow is possible. The pipeline can be run end-to-end without intervention or
with selective oversight (e.g. reviewing or overriding individual descriptors or
workshop phases). Parallel runs for “scenario ensembles” [20] require minimal
additional effort (but increase computational time).
The framework is demonstrated in a practical example that runs the scenario
generation pipeline for Germany’s energy transition to 2050, given European
and global context. Germany aims for net-zero by 2045 and has set ambitious
2030 targets, but current progress is mixed [21]. It is the focal country here,
2

with power, buildings, transport, and industry in scope and European and
global factors as drivers. Target region(s), time horizon, context, and panel
expertise can be varied, making the approach suitable for a broader range of
applications. The following section outlines the methodological pipeline in
sequence.
2. Methods
The framework comprises four linked stages: an AI-led CIB workshop that
elicits descriptors, states, and cross-impacts; a stochastic CIB analysis with
dynamic pathways and shock mechanisms; an AI-led MCDA workshop for
pathway selection; and a final quantification workshop that translates the se-
lected pathway into model-ready inputs. Whilst the design is agnostic to the
underlying LLM, the present implementation was run with Gemini 3 Flash
Preview [22].
The section is organised as follows. Section 2.1 describes the AI-led CIB
workshop protocol and outputs. Section 2.2 then specifies the CIB analysis,
including uncertainty treatment, structural and dynamic shocks, and path-
way simulation over the time grid. Appendix A details the AI-led MCDA
workshop and pathway selection protocol, and Appendix B details the quan-
tification workshop and translation of pathway states into numerical inputs.
It must be noted that CIB consistency in the impact-balance sense does not
guarantee full narrative coherence. Given this, the quantified scenario re-
mains conditional on the agreed workshop specification and on subsequent
panel choices. In the present implementation, key stages, including quan-
tification, are executed autonomously by AI panels; however, facilitator or
expertinterventioncanbeintroducedatselectedstepswherecloseralignment
with particular assessment models or storyline is required. The framework
nevertheless remains cost-effective and flexible, since panel composition, do-
main coverage, and study boundaries can be adjusted via prompts without
additional data.
Beyond these implementation choices, the framework offers what may be
termed a “Glass Box” validation standard. Full deliberative transcripts are
3

retained (in the present application they exceed 250,000 words), thereby al-
lowing a step-by-step audit of every decision, score, and quantification step
and supporting intervention at each stage. Accompanying resources offer ac-
cess to these transcripts. The following sections are organised to mirror the
model workflow, and the transcripts are structured by workshop and phase
(e.g.CIBphases1-5, MCDAphasesA0-E,quantificationphasesA-E),sothat
each subsection and phase can be traced in the accompanying materials. It
must be stressed that this level of transparency is uncommon in scenario
generation at present. The following subsection therefore begins with the
elicitation design that provides the foundational inputs for all downstream
stages.
2.1. AI-led Cross-Impact Balance workshop
The workshop follows a CIB design [1] for eliciting plausible socio-technical
futuresforGermany’senergytransitionto2050withinaEuropeanandglobal
context. The central question is as follows: what consistent futures are plau-
sible, given the interplay of policy, technology, infrastructure, society, and
international drivers? The aim is to identify the factors that matter, define
their possible states, and judge how they influence one another. The result
of the workshop is a set of agreed outputs that support the construction
of internally consistent scenarios and pathways for use in energy modelling
and related analysis. The focus here is on the methodological design of the
workshop and, in particular, on the representation of the panel of experts
as a single AI system that simulates multiple domain experts1and reaches
consensus on each workshop item.
The workshop is organised in five phases, each of which builds on the agreed
outcomes of the previous phase. The first phase establishes a common under-
standing of the workshop scope, horizon, and panel protocol. In the second
phase, the panel selects which factors (descriptors) to include for the central
question, up to a method-defined maximum of key factors. Descriptors may
be reworded or clarified. This yields an agreed set of descriptors that drives
all subsequent phases. In the third phase, for each agreed descriptor, the

the full specification required for building CIB scenarios and pathways.
The AI panel comprises five experts with predefined domains of expertise.
The first expert addresses policy and regulation: German and EU climate
andenergypolicy, targets, carbonpricing, regulatoryframework, andpermit-
ting. The second addresses technology and supply: renewables deployment,
technology costs, storage, hydrogen, negative emission technologies, supply
chains, and bioenergy. The third addresses infrastructure and markets: grid
flexibility, European grid integration, electrification, industrial demand, fos-
sil prices, the role of gas, and investment. The fourth addresses society
and behaviour: public acceptance, consumer behaviour, land-use conflict,
labour, and skills. The fifth addresses European and global context: EU
policy alignment, international coordination, energy security pressure, and
decarbonisation outcomes.
The number of experts on the AI panel, as well as their specific domains of
expertise, can be adjusted as required to suit the needs of the application.
This flexibility is illustrated in later sections of the modelled pipeline. The
panel is given a common reference context, a limited shared baseline (scope,
horizon, terminology). Experts are instructed to draw on their own domain
knowledge and may extend or refine this baseline with evidence or framings
from their respective fields.
A key feature of the approach is that the AI experts engage in elaborate
discussions amongst themselves. They argue points, challenge each other’s

In standard (global) CIB succession, each iteration computes impact bal-
ances from the current scenario and updates descriptors simultaneously to
their highest-scoring states (with deterministic tie handling), until a fixed-
point or cyclic attractor is reached. In the extended analysis, this rule is
augmented by uncertainty and shock terms and, where applicable, feasibil-
ity constraints on admissible successor states. Repeated updating in this
manner eventually settles on a fixed scenario or a small cycle; these are
the attractors implied by the cross-impact judgements. The foregoing de-

fixed CIM. The analysis employed here extends this by using PyCIB [24],

gether with structural and dynamic shocks for robustness.
Given the outputs from the workshop, a simulation-first probabilistic CIB
approach is employed to generate dynamic multi-period pathways. Specifi-
cally, instead of relying on the enumeration of all CIB-consistent scenarios
(which yields a static set and is feasible only for small spaces) or on the
estimation of attractor weights alone (which fails to produce time-evolving
pathways), a large number of independent Monte Carlo runs are performed
over the time gridT. For each run, a CIM is sampled based on the workshop
confidence levels. The system is subsequently evolved period by period via
succession, cyclic transitions, and shocks. This process ensures that each run
yields a single pathway (a linked sequence of scenarios overT).
This approach is selected because the scenario space is extensive. Moreover,
the downstream MCDA workshop requires pathway-level outputs (linked
timelines) to facilitate the selection of candidate futures. The system com-
prises the agreed 15 descriptors (three states each), and covers the time grid
T. Judgement uncertainty is confidence-coded. That is, for each cell of the
CIM the workshop agrees both a scoreµ(the point estimate for that cell)
and a confidence code (1 to 5, where 5 denotes very high confidence). The
confidence code determines a per-cell standard deviationσ, with higher con-

confidence 1). Each CIM cell is then sampled around its point estimateµ
using the confidence-derived uncertainty scaleσ, with support clipped to the
CIB score range[−3,+3]; the implementation allows Gaussian or Student-t
draws, and in this application Student-t(5 d.f.) is used for structural per-
turbations.
The workshop agreed to scaleσby period using a multiplicative factor (e.g.
1.0 at 2025, increasing to 1.5 at 2050), so that uncertainty widens for more
distant periods. A sampled matrix is drawn for each run (or per time step
whenσis scaled by period). Where dynamic shocks are present, the within-

All inputs to the CIB analysis come from the workshop outlined in the pre-
vious subsection. They are the set of descriptors and their discrete states,
the CIM (scores and confidence per source-target pair), the baseline scenario
(initial state per descriptor in the first period, 2025), domain rules (forbidden
pairs, implications), the time gridT, cyclic transition parameters (stay, step,
step2, drift per cyclic descriptor, as defined above), and the final-phase op-
tions (structural and dynamic shock scales, cyclic parameters, and metadata
such as endogenous/exogenous classification and mediated pathways for re-
porting). All of these are decided by the workshop participants. The PyCIB
package [24] can also compute diagnostics (e.g. near-miss rates, event-rate
confidence intervals, and undersampling warnings) from the pathway and
scenario outputs for use when low-probability or marginal-consistency be-
haviour is of interest; the present application does not report them in the
main pipeline. The analysis thus produces a large number of dynamic path-
way runs, from which candidate pathways are selected for the MCDA work-
shop (e.g. by frequency at 2050 and diversity of outcomes).
A general caveat applies here. CIB identifies scenarios that are internally
consistent in the sense of impact balance (each descriptor is in the state that
best fits the cross-impact judgements). That consistency does not, however,
guarantee that the resulting storylines are free of narrative tensions [4]. For
example, the agreed descriptor set and cross-impacts may embed assump-
tions or framings that conflict with one another when read as a coherent
narrative. The trajectory implied by a pathway may combine states that are
individually consistent yet jointly difficult to justify in storyline form. Such
tensions, where they arise, are carried forward in the pipeline. The candidate
pathways passed to the MCDA workshop, and hence the pathway selected
for quantification, inherit the narrative structure (and any latent tensions)
of the CIB outputs.
The quantified scenario that emerges at the end of the pipeline is therefore
conditional on both the CIB specification and the downstream choices made
by the AI panels. In the current implementation the AI expert panels work
through the pipeline autonomously, without facilitator or participant inter-
vention. The results could therefore be improved upon at each step through
targeted intervention by a facilitator or by domain experts (e.g. to validate or
refine descriptors, cross-impacts, MCDA criteria and weights, or quantified
11

assumptions). Users of the approach should remain aware that consistency
in the CIB sense is a necessary but not sufficient condition for narrative co-
herence, and that checking or refining the storyline at selected stages (e.g.
after CIB or after MCDA) may be advisable when the scenario is intended
for communication or decision support.
Recall that Appendix A details the AI-led MCDA workshop and the pathway
selection protocol, while Appendix B describes the quantification workshop
and the process of translating pathway states into numerical inputs. The
following section outlines selected results from each stage of the pipeline.
3. Results
The pipeline comprises four stages. Here, a pathway is a linked sequence of
scenarios over the time horizon (one state per descriptor per period), and a
descriptor is a factor with a set of discrete ordinal states (see Methods). The
AI-panel CIB workshop establishes the scenario framework: factors (descrip-
tors), their possible states, and the cross-impact matrix encoding how those
states influence one another. The CIB analysis then produces an ensemble of
internally consistent pathways over the time horizon. The MCDA workshop
selects one pathway from that ensemble, with a documented rationale. The
quantification workshop translates it into model-ready inputs: central trajec-
tories and uncertainty ranges for key dimensions. Two figures summarise the
results. Figure 1 illustrates the shock mechanisms. Figure 2 presents results
by stage: Panels (a) and (b) show CIB analysis; (c) and (d) show MCDA;
and (e) to (g) show quantification. The subsections describe each stage in
turn; the final subsection gives the pathway narrative, synthesis, and caveats.
3.1. AI-panel CIB workshop and analysis
The AI-panel CIB workshop (Sect. 2.1), run with five simulated experts with
predefined domains of expertise (e.g. one for policy and regulation, one for
technology and supply, and so on), produced the agreed descriptors, states,
and cross-impact matrix. The workshop agreed on 15 descriptors, each with
three ordinal states (e.g. Low, Medium, High, or method-specific labels such
as Net-zero aligned, Medium emissions, High emissions) and brief defini-
tions. The set includes, for example, Decarbonisation outcome (Germany’s
aggregate greenhouse gas emissions trajectory to 2050), Policy stringency
12

(strength of climate and energy policy), Hydrogen role (extent of hydrogen’s
role in the energy system), and Renewables deployment (extent of renewables
in the energy system). The full list and the pairwise cross-impact scores are
given in the Methods and the accompanying resources. The CIB analysis
(Sect. 2.2) takes those outputs and runs a Monte Carlo pathway simulation
(many random runs over the time horizon), yielding a large ensemble of in-
ternally consistent pathways.
TheCIBanalysisalsousestwostochasticshockmechanismstostress-testthe
robustness of consistent scenarios (formal definition in Methods Sect. 2.2).
Figure 1 illustrates them. Structural shocks perturb the workshop-agreed
CIM and stress-test whether scenarios remain consistent when the influence
table is perturbed away from the elicited central estimate. Panels (a)-(c)
of the figure show the base CIM, the structural shock, and the difference
(shocked minus base). Node size in (a)-(c) uses a common scale (total out-
going impact strength, i.e. how strongly each descriptor influences others),
so the effect of the structural shock on descriptor strength is visible in (b),
whilst (c) highlights which links changed most.
Dynamic shocks, as illustrated in Panel (d) of Figure 1, differ in that they
do not alter the CIM. Instead, they introduce random perturbations to the
impact scores when the succession operator updates each descriptor to its
best-fitting state within each period. They essentially impose time-varying
disturbances that can nudge the balance between closely competing states
and occasionally induce state switching within a pathway, with persistence
across periods given by an AR(1) (first-order autoregressive) structure (so
that shocks in one period tend to carry over to the next). That is, structural
shocks examine how robust scenarios are to errors in the elicited influence
table, whilst dynamic shocks examine how small perturbations during suc-
cession can alter which scenario is realised, a stylised representation of the
sensitivity of pathways to stochastic influences along the timeline. These
mechanisms allow scenario robustness and pathway diversity to be explored.

3.4. Pathway narrative and synthesis
The narrative of the selected pathway is summarised as follows. It is a net-
zero-aligned, hydrogen-limited pathway in which policy stringency and car-
bon price tighten late, coincident with the final push towards net-zero. The
pathway traces Germany’s energy transition from 2025 to 2050. The narra-

through 2040-2045 (tighter policy and financing), and a deeply decarbonised
end state with hydrogen limited throughout. “Net-zero aligned” is reflected
in the agreed emissions level and in the combination of policy, technology
cost, and price states. “Medium emissions” is reflected in the sustained level
over 2025-2035. The experts’ plausibility rules (e.g. coherence between pol-
icy stringency, renewables deployment, and decarbonisation outcome) are
respected in the narrative.

4. Conclusions
To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this analysis is the first of its kind
to use an AI panel of experts for structured expert elicitation and decision-
making within the context of socio-technical energy scenario building. Un-
like generative AI applications that design or discover [e.g. 27], this approach
uses AI for elicitation, consensus-building, and decision-making within es-
tablished methods. That is, no prior work is known to have applied such
an AI panel within Cross-Impact Balance (CIB) or multi-criteria decision
analysis (MCDA) settings to produce agreed multi-expert outputs for the
energy transition or other domains. Moreover, the explicit consideration of
stochastic structural and dynamic shocks that can stress-test scenario ro-
bustness and induce state switching, applied within dynamic multi-period
pathway analysis in CIB, is novel to energy scenario generation and to CIB
analysis itself. Thereby, it captures edge cases that might be smoothed over
20

in a conventional consensus process.
Beyond the present application, the approach offers flexibility in scenario
framing. In the implementation reported here, the AI experts select the
main descriptors, pathways, and related variables autonomously, on the ba-
sis of the common context and a broadly defined main scenario question.
The same design nevertheless admits a more directed use. The workshop
prompts can be tailored so that the panel is steered towards a particular
scenario family or storyline (e.g. an instance in which there is more focus
on direct air capture and storage, or one in which demand reduction and
sufficiency play a dominant role).
More generally, the approach makes high-quality socio-technical scenarios ac-
cessible to under-resourced regions (e.g. the Global South) by using synthetic
expertise at near-zero marginal cost, reducing the dominance of well-funded
institutions in scenario generation, and enabling analyses that previously
lacked expert input. The framework can also produce a new, internally con-
sistent scenario landscape in days instead of months, turning scenario plan-
ning from a slow, periodic exercise into a responsive tool that keeps assess-
ment models updated despite rapid socio-economic and geopolitical change.
Such a capability enables policymakers to explore how different panel com-
positions (e.g. NGOs versus industry) affect pathway construction and se-
lection, acting as a “wind tunnel” for exploratory policy stress-testing that
would be too costly and complex with conventional expert panels. That is,
this capability effectively creates “Virtual AI-Led Decision Laboratories”, as
demonstrated by the MCDA workshop’s configurable stakeholder personas.
Assessment modellers also obtain trajectories and uncertainty ranges, to-
gether with the pathway narrative and MCDA rationale, for direct use in
their models and for communicating scenario assumptions.
Given that MCDA and CIB are widely used and the constraints (cost, time,
transparency) are common across expert-elicitation work, the AI-driven ap-
proach can be applied beyond energy to domains such as urban planning,
land use, climate adaptation, healthcare, and environmental management.
The approach is flexible. The number and domains of AI experts, research
framework, and temporal or spatial boundaries can be changed via prompts
without extra data, providing a cost-effective way to add AI expertise to
expert elicitation and decision support. Parallel pipelines for scenario en-
21

sembles require minimal reconfiguration within the same framework, and
CIB, MCDA, fuzzy cognitive maps, Delphi, Sustainable Development Goal
assessment (e.g. using CIB to model goal interactions and their evolution
over time), and similar methods can be attached at minimal additional cost
to analyses that previously lacked such inputs.
Appendix A. AI-led multi-criteria decision analysis workshop
This AI expert-led stakeholder workshop uses multi-criteria decision analy-

a small set of candidate pathways produced by the CIB analysis outlined
in the previous subsection. The workshop uses a simple additive weighting
(SAW) approach: each pathway is scored on agreed criteria, persona-specific
criterion weights are applied, and weighted totals are averaged across per-
sonas to rank pathways. The stakeholder elicitation protocol is method-
agnostic. That is, elicited criteria, weights, and pathway scores can be
post-processed with alternative MCDA aggregators (e.g., TOPSIS, VIKOR,
PROMETHEE), subject to method-specific assumptions such as normalisa-
tion, criterion polarity, and preference-threshold settings.
One AI simulates multiple participants and reaches consensus on each item
(Sect. 2.1). Here the panel comprises ten stakeholder personas (policy and
regulation, industryandutilities, civilsocietyandNGOs, gridandinfrastruc-

labour and unions, regional and subnational, and environment and nature),
distinct from the five CIB domain experts, and the task is pathway selection
rather than CIB elicitation.
In the present application, candidate pathways from the CIB analysis are
first narrowed using their frequency and diversity of outcomes across the
ensemble; they are then screened for plausibility before stakeholder compar-
ison. The screening excludes pathways with problematic temporal patterns,
such as backsliding after improvement, implausible endpoint combinations,
late-rush transitions, or large discontinuous shifts that lack a credible nar-

that the panel can compare multiple plausible futures, including at least two

structure.title: Preface
structure.summary:
This document introduces a novel AI-based framework for generating socio-technical scenarios and providing decision guidance, particularly for complex transformation pathways like achieving net-zero emissions. The core innovation is the use of AI-simulated expert and stakeholder panels to overcome the limitations of traditional, resource-intensive scenario generation methods.

The main points covered are:

*   **Addressing Bottlenecks in Scenario Generation:** The paper highlights the challenges of conventional scenario generation, including high resource demands, limited internal consistency, lack of diverse expert perspectives, and insufficient stress-testing.
*   **AI-Simulated Expert Panels:** The framework utilizes an AI model to simulate domain experts who collaboratively define scenario descriptors, their states, and the interactions between them.
*   **Probabilistic Cross-Impact Balance (CIB) Analysis:** This method is employed to generate internally consistent pathways. The AI panel uses stochastic shocks to assess the robustness and diversity of these pathways.
*   **AI-Simulated Stakeholder Panel for Decision Making:** An AI stakeholder panel uses multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) to select a preferred pathway, explicitly addressing conflicting criteria.
*   **AI Expert Panel for Quantification:** Another AI expert panel translates the chosen pathway into quantitative inputs suitable for modeling.
*   **Proof of Concept and Application:** The framework is demonstrated using Germany's energy transition as a case study, showcasing its scalability and applicability to other countries or regions.
*   **Virtual AI-Led Decision Laboratories:** The approach enables exploratory policy stress-testing and provides a method for rapid, structured expert elicitation and decision support in various domains.
*   **Methodological Stages:** The paper outlines a four-stage methodological pipeline: AI-led CIB workshop, stochastic CIB analysis with dynamic pathways and shocks, AI-led MCDA workshop for pathway selection, and a final quantification workshop.
*   **Flexibility and Intervention:** The framework is designed to be flexible, allowing for facilitator or expert intervention at any stage, enabling hybrid workflows.
*   **"Glass Box" Validation:** The approach aims for transparency by providing full deliberative transcripts and documented reasoning at each step.

structure.title: Methods
structure.summary:
This partial document describes a methodological framework for generating plausible socio-technical futures, specifically focusing on Germany's energy transition to 2050 within a European and global context. The framework is designed to be flexible and applicable to a broader range of scenarios by allowing variations in target regions, time horizons, context, and panel expertise.

The core of the methodology comprises four linked stages:

1.  **AI-led CIB workshop:** This initial stage uses Artificial Intelligence (AI) to elicit key descriptors (factors), their possible states, and the cross-impacts between them.
2.  **Stochastic CIB analysis:** This stage involves a dynamic analysis of the elicited cross-impacts, incorporating uncertainty, structural shocks, and dynamic shock mechanisms to simulate pathways over time.
3.  **AI-led MCDA workshop:** An AI-driven Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) workshop is used to select the most plausible pathways from the simulated options.
4.  **Quantification workshop:** The final stage translates the selected pathway into model-ready inputs for further analysis.

The document emphasizes the transparency of the framework, referring to it as a "Glass Box" validation standard. It retains full deliberative transcripts of the AI panel's decisions, scores, and quantification steps, allowing for a detailed audit and intervention at each stage. The implementation uses Gemini 3 Flash Preview, but the design is agnostic to the underlying AI model. The AI panel simulates multiple domain experts to reach consensus. The document also details the organization of the AI-led Cross-Impact Balance (CIB) workshop, outlining its five phases, from establishing scope to selecting descriptors and defining their states and interrelationships.

nodes.title: AI-led Cross-Impact Balance workshop
nodes.summary:
This partial document describes a methodology for generating socio-technical futures for Germany's energy transition to 2050, focusing on transparency and an AI-led approach. The main points covered are:

*   **Transparency and Auditability:** The process generates extensive transcripts (over 250,000 words) allowing for a step-by-step audit of every decision, score, and quantification. The structure mirrors the model workflow, with transcripts organized by workshop and phase for traceability.
*   **AI-led Cross-Impact Balance (CIB) Workshop:**
    *   This workshop elicits plausible socio-technical futures by identifying key factors (descriptors), their possible states, and their interdependencies.
    *   It uses an AI system simulating multiple domain experts to reach consensus on workshop items.
    *   The workshop is structured in five phases: establishing scope, selecting descriptors, defining states, scoring cross-impacts, and defining baseline scenarios and dynamic elements.
    *   The AI panel consists of five experts with predefined domains (policy, technology, infrastructure, society, global context), adjustable as needed.
    *   A key feature is the AI experts' simulated elaborate discussions, arguments, and challenges to surface different perspectives before reaching a reasoned consensus.
*   **Cross-Impact Balance (CIB) Analysis:**
    *   This section details the core CIB method, which uses a cross-impact matrix (CIM) populated by workshop judgments to define pairwise influence scores between descriptor states.
    *   It explains how scenarios are constructed and how consistency is achieved (a scenario is consistent if each descriptor is in the state that best fits the cross-impact judgments).
    *   The analysis extends standard CIB by incorporating confidence-coded judgment uncertainty and structural/dynamic shocks for robustness.
    *   A simulation-first probabilistic CIB approach using Monte Carlo runs generates dynamic multi-period pathways, rather than relying solely on static scenario enumeration.
    *   The process involves sampling CIMs based on confidence levels, evolving scenarios period by period, and incorporating structural shocks (perturbations to CIM entries) and dynamic shocks (additions to impact scores during succession) to explore robustness and pathway diversity.
    *   Cyclic descriptors and domain rules (forbidden state combinations) are also incorporated.
*   **General Caveats:** The document highlights that CIB consistency (impact balance) does not guarantee narrative coherence, and potential tensions in storylines can be carried forward. It suggests that refining narratives at selected stages might be advisable.
*   **Pipeline Stages:** The overall pipeline comprises four stages: the AI-panel CIB workshop, CIB analysis, an AI-led Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) workshop (detailed in Appendix A), and a quantification workshop (detailed in Appendix B). The results section will summarize findings from each stage.

structure.title: Results
structure.summary:
This partial document describes a multi-stage pipeline for generating and analyzing future scenarios. The main points covered are:

*   **Caveats on Narrative Coherence:** Users are cautioned that consistency (CIB sense) is necessary but not sufficient for narrative coherence, and that refining storylines at certain stages is recommended for communication or decision support.
*   **Appendices:** References are made to Appendices A and B for details on the AI-led MCDA workshop, pathway selection, quantification workshop, and translating pathway states into numerical inputs.
*   **Pipeline Stages and Definitions:** The document outlines a four-stage pipeline:
    *   **AI-panel CIB workshop and analysis:** Establishes the scenario framework (factors/descriptors, states, cross-impact matrix) and produces an ensemble of internally consistent pathways.
    *   **MCDA workshop:** Selects one pathway from the ensemble with a documented rationale.
    *   **Quantification workshop:** Translates the selected pathway into model-ready inputs (central trajectories and uncertainty ranges).
*   **Results Summary:** Two figures are mentioned to summarize results: Figure 1 on shock mechanisms and Figure 2 presenting results by stage (CIB, MCDA, quantification).
*   **Detailed Description of CIB Workshop:** The AI-panel CIB workshop involved simulated experts and resulted in 15 descriptors, each with three ordinal states and definitions. Examples of descriptors like "Decarbonisation outcome" and "Policy stringency" are provided.

nodes.title: AI-panel CIB workshop and analysis
nodes.summary:
This partial document describes a multi-stage pipeline for generating and selecting future scenarios, likely for policy or decision-making. The main points covered are:

*   **Pipeline Stages:** The pipeline consists of four stages:
    *   **AI-panel CIB workshop and analysis:** This stage establishes the scenario framework by defining factors (descriptors) and their possible states, and a cross-impact matrix (CIM) that encodes interdependencies between these states. It then uses a Monte Carlo simulation to generate an ensemble of internally consistent pathways. Two types of stochastic shocks (structural and dynamic) are used to stress-test the robustness and diversity of these scenarios.
    *   **AI-panel MCDA workshop:** This stage selects a single preferred pathway from the ensemble generated by the CIB analysis. This selection involves narrowing down to candidate pathways and then deliberating to reach a consensus, documenting the rationale and trade-offs.
    *   **Quantification workshop:** This stage translates the selected pathway into model-ready inputs, including central trajectories and uncertainty ranges for key dimensions.
    *   **Pathway narrative, synthesis, and caveats:** The final stage involves presenting the chosen pathway, summarizing the findings, and outlining any limitations or assumptions.

*   **Key Concepts:**
    *   **Descriptors:** Factors with discrete ordinal states that represent aspects of the scenario (e.g., Decarbonisation outcome, Policy stringency).
    *   **Cross-Impact Matrix (CIM):** A matrix that quantifies how the state of one descriptor influences the state of another.
    *   **Pathways:** Linked sequences of scenarios over a time horizon, with one state per descriptor per period.
    *   **Consistency (CIB sense):** A measure of internal coherence within a pathway based on the CIM.
    *   **Narrative Coherence:** A broader concept of how well a scenario tells a believable and understandable story, which is related to but distinct from CIB consistency.
    *   **Stochastic Shocks:** Mechanisms (structural and dynamic) used to test the sensitivity and robustness of scenarios to perturbations in the CIM or during pathway evolution.

*   **Results Presentation:** The document refers to figures that illustrate the results of each stage, including shock mechanisms, the distribution of pathways across states over time, co-occurrence of states, and the selection of a preferred pathway.

*   **Caveats:** Users are reminded that CIB consistency is necessary but not sufficient for narrative coherence, and that refining the storyline at certain stages might be beneficial for communication or decision support.

nodes.title: AI-panel MCDA workshop
nodes.summary:
The document describes a process for generating and selecting socio-technical energy scenarios for Germany's energy transition. It covers three main stages:

1.  **Scenario Ensemble Generation (CIB analysis):** This stage uses expert judgments to create a range of plausible future pathways, considering factors like policy stringency, renewables deployment, and grid development. It analyzes how often different states (e.g., "Net-zero aligned," "High policy stringency") co-occur over time, highlighting the coherence between certain descriptors. This helps define internally consistent decarbonization assumptions for assessment modelers.

2.  **AI-panel Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) Workshop:** This workshop narrows down the scenario ensemble to a few candidate pathways. Through deliberation, it selects a single preferred pathway based on criteria like feasibility, ambition, and equity. The process captures value conflicts between simulated stakeholder personas and documents the trade-offs made to reach a consensus, providing an audit trail for the chosen pathway.

3.  **AI-panel Scenario Quantification:** The selected pathway is translated from qualitative states (e.g., "Medium policy stringency") into numerical values usable by assessment models. This stage also incorporates uncertainty ranges assigned by experts, which can be used as inputs or bounds in modeling. The document illustrates these quantified results with examples of CO2 emissions, carbon prices, technology costs, and policy stringency over time.

nodes.title: AI-panel scenario quantification
nodes.summary:
This partial document describes the process of selecting and quantifying a specific pathway for energy transition modeling. It covers the following main points:

*   **Score Matrix and Pathway Selection:** Panel (d) of Figure 2 shows a score matrix used in a workshop to select a pathway based on agreed scores across various criteria and personas. This matrix serves as an audit trail, documenting the rationale behind pathway choices.
*   **AI-Panel Scenario Quantification:** The selected pathway is then quantified into numerical forms suitable for assessment models. This involves translating qualitative states (e.g., policy stringency levels) into single numeric values per period. The document explains that trajectories can exhibit flat segments and step changes due to this discrete state-to-value mapping, and that smoothed curves in figures are for display purposes.
*   **Presentation of Results (Figure 2 Panels e-g):** Panels (e) and (f) display central trajectories of key variables (emissions, carbon price, technology cost index, WACC) as percentage changes from 2025. Panel (g) shows descriptor states (public acceptance, policy stringency) over time, also smoothed for display. Uncertainty ranges assigned by AI experts are also presented.
*   **Detailed Pathway Narrative and Cross-Impacts:** The document provides a detailed narrative for a specific pathway, explaining the evolution of CO2 emissions, policy stringency, technology costs, investment availability, and public acceptance. It highlights how these descriptors interact and influence each other, including asymmetric feedback loops and the concept of cyclic descriptors.
*   **Synthesis of the Methodological Pipeline:** The document concludes by summarizing how Figure 2 visually traces the entire methodological pipeline, from initial workshops and Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) to the final quantification, demonstrating how broad ensembles of futures are narrowed down to a single, justified trajectory.

nodes.title: Pathway narrative and synthesis
nodes.summary:
This partial document describes a specific pathway for Germany's energy transition from 2025 to 2050, focusing on a net-zero-aligned, hydrogen-limited scenario. Key points include:

*   **Public Acceptance:** This factor is modeled as "cyclic," meaning it can change between periods due to discourse, events, and trust. In this pathway, public acceptance rises from 2025 to 2030, remains high until 2045, and then steps down in the final period, potentially due to stochastic transitions.
*   **Pathway Narrative:** The selected pathway is characterized by a late tightening of policy stringency and carbon prices, coinciding with the final push towards net-zero. It involves a decisive shift in 2035, consolidation from 2040-2045, and a deeply decarbonized end state with limited hydrogen use.
*   **Methodological Pipeline:** The document outlines a step-by-step process from initial analysis and multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) workshops to final quantification, leading to a single, justified trajectory.
*   **Caveats and Limitations:** The document acknowledges methodological artifacts like flat segments in trajectories, the interpretive nature of causal language in the storyline, and the conditional nature of the results based on the AI-expert panel setup.
*   **Novelty of Approach:** The analysis is highlighted as the first to use an AI panel of experts for structured elicitation and decision-making in socio-technical energy scenario building, specifically within Cross-Impact Balance (CIB) and MCDA settings. The explicit consideration of stochastic shocks and state switching in dynamic multi-period pathway analysis is also presented as novel.

structure.title: Conclusions
structure.summary:
This partial document discusses the application of an AI expert panel for socio-technical energy scenario building. Key points include:

*   **Methodology and Data Provision:** The document explains how the AI panel's outputs, derived from a pathway narrative and selection rationale, provide quantitative data and contextual information for assessment modellers.
*   **Caveats and Interpretations:** It highlights important caveats regarding the results, such as methodological artifacts in discrete-state designs, the interpretive nature of causal language, and the conditional nature of specific results on the current setup.
*   **Novelty of the Approach:** The analysis is presented as the first to use an AI panel for structured expert elicitation and decision-making in energy scenario building, particularly within Cross-Impact Balance (CIB) and multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) settings. The explicit consideration of stochastic shocks and dynamic pathway analysis is also noted as novel.
*   **Flexibility and Accessibility:** The approach is described as flexible, allowing for directed use and tailored prompts to steer the panel towards specific scenario families. It also aims to make high-quality scenarios accessible to under-resourced regions and to accelerate scenario planning.
*   **"Virtual AI-Led Decision Laboratories":** The framework enables policymakers to explore the impact of different panel compositions and act as a "wind tunnel" for policy stress-testing.
*   **Broader Applicability:** The AI-driven approach is deemed applicable beyond energy to domains like urban planning, climate adaptation, and healthcare, due to its flexibility in adapting parameters and integrating with various analytical methods.
*   **AI-led MCDA Workshop:** A specific appendix details an AI expert-led MCDA workshop using a simple additive weighting approach for pathway selection, simulating multiple stakeholder personas. The process involves screening candidate pathways for plausibility before stakeholder comparison.

structure.title: AI-led multi-criteria decision analysis workshop
structure.summary:
This partial document describes two appendices related to an AI-led process for pathway selection and quantification.

Appendix A details an AI-led multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) workshop. This workshop uses a Simple Additive Weighting (SAW) approach to select a preferred pathway from a set generated by a previous analysis (CIB). The process involves defining stakeholder personas, agreeing on evaluation criteria and their weights for each persona, scoring candidate pathways against these criteria, and then aggregating these scores and weights to rank the pathways. The final selection is made through deliberation based on this ranking. The appendix also outlines alternative, simpler rule-based selection methods that can be used if a deliberative rationale is not required.

Appendix B introduces an AI-led scenario quantification workshop. This workshop takes the pathway selected in Appendix A and translates it into quantitative inputs for assessment models.

structure.title: AI-led scenario quantification
structure.summary:
This document describes a two-phase process for developing quantitative scenarios for assessment models. The first phase, detailed in Appendix A, involves a Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) workshop to select a preferred pathway from a set of potential trajectories. This selection is based on panel deliberation and scoring against agreed criteria, with the output being a single selected pathway and a 2050 scenario snapshot. The process emphasizes transparency by recording the criteria, weights, and scores used. An alternative to the MCDA workshop is a simpler, rule-based selection for applications not requiring a documented rationale for pathway choice.

Appendix B details the second phase: AI-led scenario quantification. This workshop translates the selected pathway from the MCDA phase into quantitative inputs for assessment models. An AI panel of experts identifies necessary variables, assigns numerical values or ranges, and generates input vectors with explicit uncertainty ranges. The process is structured in phases: context and pathway presentation, agreement on model-input dimensions and a translation matrix, generation and review of a baseline input table, and finally, agreement on uncertainty ranges, extreme scenarios, and alternative pathways. The output is a quantified pathway suitable for assessment models, along with uncertainty bounds and additional scenarios for sensitivity analysis. The document also notes that the quantification step can result in discrete, potentially volatile, period-to-period steps in the quantified trajectory, which modellers may need to interpolate.
